query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating is governed by the formation of a stable oxide layer at the coating surface, which acts as a barrier to abrasive wear and fatigue wear, and this stability is enhanced by the coating's high hardness and fine grain size.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing at 500 °C with a normal load of 10 N and a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s
generation.mechanism: The stable oxide layer acts as a barrier to abrasive wear and fatigue wear, reducing the wear rate of the coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: A 20% reduction in wear rate compared to the untreated coating
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 400-600 °C, Normal load range: 5-15 N, Sliding speed range: 0.05-0.2 m/s
generation.uncertainty: The actual wear rate reduction may vary depending on the specific coating composition, substrate material, and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature wear testing with varying heat treatment temperatures and times
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate of the heat-treated coating is not reduced by at least 15% compared to the untreated coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 14 shows the wear amount and wear rate of CS and HVOF coatings heat treated at different temperatures. In general, the variations of the two coatings are relatively consistent. The wear rates of the two coatings without heat treatment are very close, which are 0.2952 mm3 m−1 N−1 and 0.3016 mm3 m−1 N−1, respectively. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of HVOF-500 °C coating. The sliding wear resistance of the CS coating is better compared to the HVOF coating. After heat treatment at 500 °C, the hardness of the HVOF coating and CS coating increases and the internal stress decreases, so the wear resistance is better. High-temperature heat treatment (700, 900 °C) leads to grain coarsening, thus reducing hardness and wear resistance. The wear rate of the HVOF-900 °C coating is the highest, about 1.1 times that of the CS-900 °C coating. The wear volume and wear rate of the substrate are 0.0275 mm3 and 0.4534 mm3 m−1 N−1, respectively. This also shows that the coatings can protect the substrate after reasonable heat treatment. The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. The wear rate for the CS and HVOF coatings reaches its the lowest point after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of the HVOF-500 °C coating. The CS coating with 500 °C vacuum heat treatment has the best wear resistance due to having the highest microhardness. The wear rates and wear amounts of the two coatings heat-treated at 700 °C and 900 °C decreases due to the decrease in microhardness. The wear mechanisms of the CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.
